newsitem.title: VATICAN: FEATURE - Pope marks 50th anniversary of priesthood.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Pope marks 50th anniversary of priesthood.

text.p: Half a century ago in a quiet ceremony in a chapel in war-ravaged Poland, a 26-year-old man was ordained a priest of the Roman Catholic Church.

Karol Wojtyla, like most men of his generation who entered the priesthood, fully expected to remain in his country for the rest of his life as a small part of a Church where authority, particularly papal authority, was unquestioned.

Today, as an ageing and fragile Pope John Paul II, Wojtyla leads a polarised Church in which hardly a week passes without a clash between his critics and supporters over his authority and the type of man who should succeed him.
Wojtyla said recently that he looks back at November 1, 1946 as the moment he decided to let "God open roads before me day by day".

As the Pope's health has deteriorated in recent years, some progressives in the 960 million member Church have openly prayed that God should inspire him to step down instead of reigning for life as Roman Catholic pontiffs traditionally do.
This, they hope, could give way to a younger, more open-minded leader.
The last Pope to resign was Celestine V in 1296, who stepped down during a turbulent period in the Church's history.
Vatican officials have all but dismissed talk of resignation, pointing out that the Pope himself said last year that only God could decide when and how his service to the Church should end.

Dissident Swiss theologian Hans Kung, who has been disciplined by the Vatican, took his 15-year offensive against the Pope a step further last week by suggesting that only his death could lead to a free choice of his successor.
Resignation, Kung suggested in an interview with Italy's Corriere della Sera newspaper, would only allow him to manipulate the election of his successor from behind the scene.

"He would do everything to aim at a successor who would be in the Wojtyla line, or someone from Opus Dei," Kung said, referring to the worldwide conservative Catholic organisation which the Pope supports.
"It must be guaranteed that the cardinals can choose a successor without manipulation, guided solely by the hand of the Holy Spirit," Kung said.
Vittorio Messori, a Roman Catholic writer who interviewed the Pope for his 1995 bestseller "Crossing the Threshold of Hope", later attacked Kung in the same newspaper.

He blasted Kung's suggestion that the Pope was cunning enough to block the work of the Holy Spirit -- which is supposed to inspire cardinals in a conclave -- as "aggression sometimes bordering on insult".
In fact, the Pope has already stacked the odds that his successor will be a conservative in his own stamp. He has named some 85 percent of the cardinals who could enter a conclave.
The high-profile and somewhat theologically esoteric duel between Kung and Messori was just a microcosm of the malaise and tension which sometimes surfaces in the Church at large.
Everywhere in parishes from Boston to Barcelona, Roman Catholics who have never heard of Kung or Messori are clashing, in their own small way, over the same big issue -- papal authority.
On the one side conservatives are unflaggingly loyal to the Pope as the man they say took a Church buffetted by the winds of liberalism since the 1960s and put it squarely back on course.

This, the conservatives say, is the only way for the Church to survive in a sea of change they feel has flawed other Christian denominations too keen to bend old rules for the sake of becoming modern.
The progressives counter that this Pope has made many of them orphans of the modern world because he refuses to budge on issues such as priestly celibacy, women's ordination and birth control.
The Pope is now in the 19th year of his history-making papacy and his declining health in recent years has also fuelled the talk of resignation, particularly if illness left him incapacitated.
The Vatican has not denied a string of recent reports that the Pope is suffering from Parkinson's disease, a potentially debilitating neurological disorder.
The Pope is determined to lead Roman Catholics into the next millennium and aides have said it is this goal that might just convince him finally to obey doctors' orders to slow down.
"We told him he had to rest," said Professor Francesco Crucitti, the surgeon who operated on the Pope, as the Pontiff left hospital in October after surgery to remove his appendix.
The Pope has since been working on a reduced schedule and aides say that the pace of his papacy will possibly never be what it once was.
After a breathless 18 years of travel that has taken him the equivalent of 25 times around the world, the stage seems set for a different form of papacy.

Since his 1978 election as the world's first non-Italian Pontiff in 450 years, the Pope has made 74 overseas journeys and 127 trips in Italy, travelled more than a million kilometres (600,000 miles) and spent the equivalent of nearly two full years outside the Vatican.
He has visited 114 of the world's 191 countries and read nearly 2,500 speeches.
There are already signs that even if he does recover fully from his health problems, the Pope intends to delegate more activities, such as secondary liturgical celebrations, to aides.
